Reinforcement Learning

  • Hebbian learning is sometimes called two-factor learning.

  • The first factor is the presynaptic activity and the second factor is the postsynaptic activity.

  • Reinforcement learning adds a third factor:

    • Did something unexpectedly good or bad happen?
    • If good, increase active weights.
    • If bad, decrease active weights.
    • This is the reinforcement signal.

Edward Thorndike

  • Edward Thorndike (1874–1949) was a psychologist who studied animal learning.

Thorndike’s Puzzle Box

  • Law of Effect (1905):
    • Behaviours followed by satisfying outcomes become more likely.
    • Behaviours followed by discomfort become less likely.

Pavlovian Conditioning

  • Ivan Pavlov (1849–1936) was a Russian physiologist who studied the physiology of digestion.

Pavlov’s Dogs

  • Pavlov’s dogs learned to salivate at the sound of a bell that was previously paired with food.

B.F. Skinner and Operant Conditioning

  • B.F. Skinner (1904–1990) formalised the concept of reinforcement as a core driver of learning.

  • Positive reinforcement: increases behavior by presenting a reward.

  • Negative reinforcement: increases behavior by removing an aversive stimulus.

Classical vs. Operant Conditioning

  • Skinner distinguished between Classical / Pavlovian conditioning and Operant / Instrumental conditioning

  • Classical conditioning: Reinforcement is uncontrollable and occurs independently of the subject’s behavior.

  • Operant conditioning: Reinforcement is controllable and occurs dependently on the subject’s behavior.

Mathematical Foundations of Associative Learning

  • Psychologists like Bush & Mosteller (1955) and Rescorla & Wagner (1972) developed formal models of stimulus-response (S-R) associative learning.

  • These models describe learning as a gradual change in associative strength driven by prediction error.

\[ \Delta V = \alpha (R - V) \]

  • \(V\) is the current associative strength and also serves as a prediction of the outcome.

  • \(R\) is the actual outcome (e.g., presence or absence of reward).

  • \(\alpha\) is a learning rate parameter,

Reinforcement Learning in Computer Science

  • In the 1980s and 1990s, Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto began formalising artificially intelligent agents that learn from reward.

  • Their models were deeply influenced by animal learning research and aimed to formalize learning mechanisms observed in nature.

  • Reinforcement learning is still an important part modern AI, including for training systems like large language models (LLMs), robotics, and game-playing agents.

Reinforcement Learning in the Brain

\[ \Delta V = \alpha (R - V) \]

  • \(\alpha\) is a learning rate parameter.

  • \(R\) is the obtained reward.

  • \(V\) is the predicted reward.

  • \((R - V)\) is the reward prediction error.

  • Easy to show that this learning rule causes \(V\) to converge to the expected value of \(R\).

Dopamine Neurons Signal Reward Prediction Error

  • If something better than expected occurs, the prediction error is positive and dopamine neurons increase firing.

  • If something worse than expected occurs, the prediction error is negative and dopamine neurons decrease firing.

  • The magnitude of the prediction error is encoded by the rate of firing of dopamine neurons.

Dopamine Neurons Signal Reward Prediction Error

Synaptic Plasiticity at Cortico-Striatal Synapses

  • The synaptic weights between the cortex and the striatum follow a three-factor learning rule.

  • Factor 1: presynaptic activity (cortical neurons).

  • Factor 2: postsynaptic activity (striatal projection neurons).

  • Factor 3: reinforcement signal provided by dopamine released into the striatum from the midbrain.

Synaptic Plasiticity at Cortico-Striatal Synapses on the Direct Pathway

  • The confluence of strong pre- and postsynaptic activity leads to activation of NMDA receptors, causing calcium influx and initiating intracellular signaling cascades, including CaMKII phosphorylation.

  • Dopamine release above baseline, typically following a positive reward prediction error, activates D1 receptors on direct pathway medium spiny neurons in the striatum, leading to phosphorylation of DARPP-32.

  • When both CaMKII and DARPP-32 are phosphorylated, this promotes synaptic potentiation, particularly via enhanced AMPA receptor trafficking and gene transcription.

  • When CaMKII is phosphorylated but DARPP-32 is not – as may occur during low or negative dopamine conditions (e.g., negative prediction error) – synaptic weakening (depression) is more likely.

Synaptic Plasiticity at Cortico-Striatal Synapses on the Indirect Pathway

  • The confluence of strong pre- and postsynaptic activity leads to activation of NMDA receptors, calcium influx, and phosphorylation of CaMKII, similar to the direct pathway.

  • Dopamine dips below baseline, typically following a negative reward prediction error, lead to reduced activation of D2 receptors on indirect pathway medium spiny neurons (MSNs), thereby disinhibiting intracellular signaling cascades that favor synaptic weakening.

  • When CaMKII is phosphorylated and D2 receptor activation is low, intracellular pathways (e.g., increased cAMP/PKA activity) facilitate long-term depression (LTD).

  • Under baseline or elevated dopamine, activation of D2 receptors suppresses these LTD pathways, making synaptic weakening less likely.

Comparing Synaptic Plasticity in Direct vs. Indirect Pathways

Feature Direct Pathway (D1 MSNs) Indirect Pathway (D2 MSNs)
Dopamine receptor D1 D2
Dopamine effect Excitatory Inhibitory
Plasticity gate Phosphorylation of DARPP-32 via D1 activation Disinhibition of LTD mechanisms when D2 is not activated
Positive RPE (↑ dopamine) Promotes LTP (via D1 + CaMKII + DARPP-32) Promotes LTD (via D2 activation and downstream signaling)
Negative RPE (↓ dopamine) Promotes LTD (CaMKII active, no D1 input) Reduces LTD, possibly permitting LTP under strong input
Outcome Strengthens rewarded actions Suppresses unrewarded actions

Reinforcement Learning Weight Update Rule

\[ \begin{align} w_{ij}(n+1) &= w_{ij}(n) \pm \alpha A_j(n) A_i(n) \delta(n) \\ \delta(n) &= r_{\text{obtained}}(n) - r_{\text{predicted}}(n) \\ r_{\text{obtained}}(n) &= \text{to be determined by the experiment} \\ r_{\text{predicted}}(n) &= \text{must be estimated from experience} \\ \end{align} \]

  • The \(\pm\) sign is meant to reflect the opposite processes along the direct and indirect pathways.

  • Here, we took the simplest Hebbian learning rule as a base, but we could have taken any of the other Hebbian learning rules as a base instead.

Estimating Predicted Reward

  • Given the learning rule above, the weight \(w_{ij}\) itself is in essence an estimate of the predicted reward.

  • However it is more common for reinforcement learning in the brain to treat the system driving actions (i.e., the weight \(w_{ij}\)) as separate from the system evaluating outcomes and generating predictions.

  • This type of separation is frequently referred to as the actor-critic model of reinforcement learning.

  • For this reason we will estimate the predicted reward separately from the weight update rule.

Estimating Predicted Reward

  • We won’t need a sophisticated model to estimate the predicted reward. The following will suffice:
r_obtained = np.zeros(n_trials) # obtained reward
r_predicted = np.zeros(n_trials) # predicted reward

alpha_pr = 0.1 # learning rate for predicted reward

for i in range(0, n_trials-1):
    # code to determine r_obtained would go here

    # update the predicted reward
    r_predicted[i+1] = r_predicted[i] + alpha_pr * (r_obtained[i] - r_predicted[i])

    # update weights with bio Hebbian learning rule modified for RL
    alpha = 1e-9; beta = 1e-9; lamb = 1e-20; theta = 1e8;

    pre = g_A[trl, :].sum()

    post_ltd_1 = np.heaviside(theta - post, 0)

    post_ltp_2 = 1.0 - np.exp(-lamb * (post - theta))

Reinforcement Learning on the Direct Pathway

    delta_w = 0.0

        delta_w += alpha * pre * post_ltp_1 * post_ltp_2 * (1 - w[trl]) * delta[trl]
    else:
        # LTD caused by stong post-synaptic activity and negative reward prediction error
        delta_w -= alpha * pre * post_ltp_1 * post_ltp_2 * (1 - w[trl]) * np.abs(delta[trl])

    # LTD also caused by weak post-synaptic activity
    delta_w -= beta * pre * post_ltd_1 * post_ltd_2 * w[trl]
